newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO top brass defer on command cutback.
newsitem.headline: NATO top brass defer on command cutback.

text.p: NATO's military chiefs of staff called on Friday for a streamlined command structure to help the alliance function in the new world order, but were forced to defer to their political superiors on how to go about it.

Stalled by a dispute between France and the United States over who should run NATO's powerful southern command in Naples, military top brass ended a two-day meeting unable to recommend an agreed plan to alliance ambassadors.

Instead, they gave the ambassadors, who as representatives of member governments set policy for the 16-nation North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, two options for restructuring NATO's European commands.

German General Klaus Naumann, chairman of NATO's military committee, said the chiefs of defence staff had agreed that the number of NATO's local headquarters should be slashed by about two-thirds to around 20 to allow the alliance to function more efficiently.
"We are about to be serious as far as lean management is concerned," Naumann told a news conference.
There was no agreement, however, about how the key regional command structure should be organised.
Naumann said a large majority of countries wanted just two European commands -- one in the Netherlands commanding the north, the other in Italy commanding the south and the Mediterranean.
The second option, which the United States has been keen to keep open, is to retain the third existing command in Britain.
Behind the disagreement lies a row between Washington and Paris over the southern command, AFSOUTH.
France is insisting that the commander of AFSOUTH must be a European, reflecting the continent's desire to develop a European security identity within the alliance.
It has said it will consider stepping back from its commitment to rejoin NATO's military command if it is not satisfied with NATO's Europeanisation.
The United States, however, has ruled out giving up the AFSOUTH command, which is responsible for the U.S. Sixth Fleet and is integral to Washington's Middle East policy.
Washington has suggested keeping the third regional command so that two of three commanders could be Europeans.

It has also agreed that the deputy supreme allied commander for Europe should remain European with new powers to coordinate European-only actions. The supreme commander, based in Mons, Belgium, is always an American.
France on Thursday appeared to tone down its demand over Naples, when Defence Minister Charles Millon told NATO parliamentarians he believed the issue could be solved.
"You know there is a discussion on this point with our American friends who have raised a number of questions. I believe they can be answered," he said.
But NATO sources said on Friday that France was still firmly committed to the idea of a European at AFSOUTH.

"France still sees it as a fundamental requirement," one source said, adding that it may be up to NATO leaders to solve the dispute at a summit next year. "It can only be sorted out at the highest political levels."

In other matters related to NATO reform, the chiefs of staff found more unity. Naumann said they had made progress in practical planning for Combined Joint Task Forces, the new system that will allow Europeans to act without the United States if necessary.
They also agreed in principle that partner countries such as Poland should have representatives at NATO headquarters as part of an enhanced Partnership for Peace programme.
